title: Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story
synopsis: Apartment 213 smells wrong again. You live in 212. The police don't listen to women who look like you in this neighborhood. You will have to be the one who is right.

nodes.text: It is in the hallway again, the same as it was in August, the same as March. Sweet at the front, and underneath it something that closes the back of your throat. The super has written refrigerator on four separate work orders this year and closed all four. Your son is eight. He has learned to hold his breath from the stairwell door to the lift, and he does it now without being told.

choices.text: Knock on 213 yourself
choices.consequence: You cross a hallway you have crossed a thousand times, and it takes you four minutes to get to the other side of it.

choices.text: Document every incident in a notebook
choices.consequence: You decide that if nobody will hear you, you will at least make it impossible for anyone to claim you never spoke.

nodes.text: He opens the door eight inches. Glasses, polite, a little embarrassed. It is the freezer, ma'am, it quit on me and I have not had the money. He apologises twice. He uses the name off your mailbox. And in the seconds the door stands open the smell comes out into the hall at full strength, and then he closes it, and he is still smiling as it shuts.

choices.text: Tell the super again, firmly
choices.consequence: You stand in the super's office until he writes something down. He writes the wrong thing, slowly, so that you will leave.

choices.text: Call the police non-emergency line
choices.consequence: You dial the number off the fridge magnet and rehearse three sentences first, so you will sound calm and not like a woman complaining.

nodes.text: You buy a black composition book at the corner store for eighty-nine cents. Date. Time. What you smelled. What came through the wall — the saw, twice, after midnight; a freezer door; a voice that stopped mid-word. By the fourth page you have stopped writing it for yourself. You are writing it for a room with a court reporter in it, and you hate that you already know that.

choices.text: Share the notebook with your sister
choices.consequence: You photocopy nine pages at the library for forty-five cents and hand them to the one person who has never told you to calm down.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself for safety
choices.consequence: You keep it under the pans in the bottom cupboard. Nobody can call you hysterical about a thing they have not read.

nodes.text: Two officers, one clipboard, no pen ever taken out of the pocket. One of them says that a lot of single men live like that. The other looks past you into your apartment, at your son on the couch, at the street out the window, and you can watch him filing you as he does it. The visit takes nine minutes. Neither of them knocks on 213.

choices.text: File a formal complaint
choices.consequence: You go downtown, wait two hours, and put your name on a form. The form has a box for race and a box for building and no box for a smell.

choices.text: Wait for a worse incident, prepared
choices.consequence: You decide the next one will be undeniable and set the notebook and the phone beside the door. Knowing it is coming does not feel like patience.

nodes.text: Denise works the city desk at the paper, mostly obituaries and school-board budgets. She listens for forty minutes without interrupting, which nobody has done. Then she asks whether she can open a file — dates, names, who you called, who called back. Somebody is finally writing it down. You get into the car afterwards and cry for three full minutes before you are able to drive home.

choices.text: Let her start a quiet file
choices.consequence: She opens a folder with your building number on the tab and puts it in a newsroom drawer. It is not nothing. It is not much either.

choices.text: Ask her to wait until you have proof
choices.consequence: You ask her to hold off, because you have been called a liar before and it left a mark. The holding off costs weeks.

nodes.text: He cannot be more than fifteen. He is on the landing with nothing to wear and no words in any language, swaying, hurt, and when you get your coat around his shoulders he takes hold of your sleeve with both hands. Two squad cars come. The man from 213 comes down in a clean shirt, calls it a lovers' quarrel, keeps his voice reasonable. The officers walk that child back through his door.

choices.text: Refuse to leave the hallway until they re-examine
choices.consequence: You stand in the hallway saying the words interpreter and ambulance until an officer tells you to go inside, ma'am. You do not go inside.

choices.text: Call your sister immediately for the story
choices.consequence: You are on the lobby payphone before the squad cars have pulled off the block, reading badge numbers to your sister off your own palm.

nodes.text: Glenda from the building next door has been calling since spring — the precinct, the field office, the mayor's line, a captain who told her to stop tying up the switchboard. She has kept every date on the back of a utility envelope. You sit at her kitchen table and put your notebook beside her envelope, and together you build one list: forty-one calls, nine departments, no callbacks.

choices.text: Take the list to a city council member
choices.consequence: You get twenty minutes with an aide who is kind, takes notes, and has no power whatsoever. He does at least keep the copy.

choices.text: Take it directly to the FBI tip line
choices.consequence: Glenda dials, because Glenda has the number memorised by now. The two of you stand in her kitchen listening to it ring.

nodes.text: Denise walks into the precinct at four on a Friday with a second reporter and a folder half an inch thick — the dates, the calls, the badge numbers, the boy on the landing. She does not raise her voice. She reads three entries aloud and asks whether the department would care to comment for Sunday. Inside about ninety seconds the desk sergeant becomes an entirely different man.

choices.text: Stay for the interview
choices.consequence: You sit down, give your name, spell it, and say all of it again on the record. It is the first time anybody has asked you to repeat anything.

choices.text: Stay anonymous; let the file speak
choices.consequence: You wait in the car with the engine running. A record can be a record without your son's address printed inside it.

nodes.text: The agent who calls back is not what you braced for. No sighing, no ma'am, no explanation of jurisdiction. She has been pulling missing-persons reports out of this half of the city for a year and she has noticed what everybody else declined to notice: the same eight blocks, the same ages, the same families told to wait and see. You hear a page turn. Then she says, tell me everything, and means it.

choices.text: Tell her everything you have
choices.consequence: You talk for two hours and read the notebook aloud from page one. At the end she says your name back to you, correctly, and spells it.

choices.text: Tell her enough to get her on a plane
choices.consequence: You give her the shape and hold back the details, because you want her here, in the hallway, smelling it herself. She books the flight.

nodes.text: It is a Monday, late, and this time the man who gets out of 213 makes it all the way to the street with a handcuff still on one wrist. This time there are three cars. And this time, because a reporter is holding a folder and an agent is holding a file and the woman in 212 is holding a notebook, nobody stands in that hallway arguing about whether it is a domestic matter.

choices.text: Watch from the hallway, calmly
choices.consequence: You stand in your own doorway with your arms folded and watch it happen. Your hands do not start shaking until an hour afterwards.

choices.text: Hold Glenda's hand
choices.consequence: You find Glenda on the front steps and take her hand, and neither of you says a word, because there is nothing the size of this.

nodes.text: Three days later: a podium, a row of flags, the chief and the mayor. Oversight. Review. Procedures under examination. Nobody says the word Laotian. Nobody says the phrase forty-one calls. Nobody says your name or Glenda's or the name of the boy on the landing. The two of you watch it on the television above the bar across the street, splitting one beer, because one beer is what is in your purse.

choices.text: Speak to a reporter outside
choices.consequence: You cross the street and give your name to a woman from Channel 6. You are on at ten for nineteen seconds, with your name spelled wrong.

choices.text: Drink the beer in silence
choices.consequence: You let the men on the television keep the room. Glenda says nothing either, and later you both regret it in almost the same words.

nodes.text: The counts multiply weekly. Names come out of the district attorney's office and then, harder, out of the families' own mouths — a dancer, a nineteen-year-old with a scholarship, a brother who never once missed a Sunday call home. Some had been reported missing for two years. You do the arithmetic on your own tenancy: twenty-six months across that hallway, and fourteen of them spent calling people who did not call back.

choices.text: Read every news report obsessively
choices.consequence: You take all three papers and clip everything. You learn the victims' names before the anchors have learned to pronounce them.

choices.text: Stop reading; protect your sleep
choices.consequence: You cancel the papers and turn the set off at six. Knowing more will not un-know any of it, and your son needs you at the table.

nodes.text: They come to the courthouse in coats too thin for November — mothers, an uncle, two brothers who flew in from three states. Somebody points you out in the corridor as the woman from 212, and then they are shaking your hand and thanking you, and you have to stand there and receive it. Gratitude, you learn that morning, is a shape grief takes when there is nowhere else for it to go.

choices.text: Stay close to the families through the trial
choices.consequence: You start driving two of the mothers in every day, and you learn their sons' names the way you know your own son's friends.

choices.text: Help them organize a memorial
choices.consequence: You find a church basement, forty chairs, and a photocopied program with every name spelled the way that family spells it.

nodes.text: A committee room with terrible acoustics, sixteen months on. You testify for nine minutes. Glenda testifies for longer and never once looks down at her notes. The two officers who walked that boy back through the door are fired in the spring, appeal in the autumn, and are reinstated with back pay the following year. One of them is later elected president of the police union.

choices.text: Push for systemic reforms
choices.consequence: You pick the boring fight: language-access rules, call-log audits, a supervisor's signature on every welfare check. Boring is what survives an election.

choices.text: Push for individual prosecution of those officers
choices.consequence: You want those two names specifically, and you spend the next three years finding out what qualified immunity is actually for.

nodes.text: He is eight and he asks it at the kitchen table with his cereal going soft: was it your fault we lived next door to him. You get down on the floor so that his eyes are above yours, and you tell him the true version — that you saw it, that you said it out loud forty-one times, and that grown-ups whose entire job was listening did not listen. He thinks. Then he asks whether they will next time.

choices.text: Promise him you'll make sure people listen next time
choices.consequence: You promise, at the kitchen table, with no idea how. He takes it as settled, which means now you are going to have to do it.

choices.text: Promise him you'll move somewhere else
choices.consequence: You promise a different hallway, a different stairwell, a window with a tree in it. He asks whether he can bring the bike.

nodes.text: It is you, Glenda, and three of the mothers, and it meets in whichever basement is free that month. You keep a phone tree, a list of which reporters return calls, and a shoebox that pays for bus fare and funeral flowers. In four years you get a language line at the precinct and a rule that a welfare check needs a supervisor's name on it. Slow. Small. Actual.

choices.text: Make this your life's work
choices.consequence: You give it the next twenty years. It takes all twenty, and you would not hand a single one of them back if offered.

choices.text: Do it for a year, then step back
choices.consequence: You give it twelve honest months and pass the phone tree to a woman with more evenings than you have. Nobody is owed your whole life.

nodes.text: Two suitcases, four boxes, and your son's bike with the streamers still on, carried down three flights to a borrowed hatchback. You hand back the keys to 212 and do not look at the door across the hall. The notebook travels in your purse, not the boxes. The new place is smaller, twenty minutes further from work, on a street where you do not yet know a single thing.

choices.text: Take a year before deciding what's next
choices.consequence: You take a job with regular hours and spend a year learning how to hear a stairwell door without standing up.

choices.text: Throw yourself into a new job
choices.consequence: You work doubles until you are too tired to lie awake, which functions beautifully for roughly seven months.

nodes.text: Ten years on, a different zip code, a recruit class at the academy across town. There is a module now on welfare checks, interpreters, and taking the complainant seriously, and in the footnotes of the policy it cites are two names and a date in 1991. You will never meet the young officer reading it. She will, one day, stand in a hallway and believe a woman. That is the whole of it.

choices.text: Make peace with the legacy
choices.consequence: You let yourself be a footnote and stop auditing the outcome. It is a kind of rest, and you have earned every hour of it.

choices.text: Stay vigilant; the work is never done
choices.consequence: You keep the numbers current and call the district commander every January, just so he knows the line still works.

nodes.text: She dies at seventy-five of the ordinary things — the heart, the lungs, a hospital room with the television bolted near the ceiling. You speak for four minutes. Half the room has stood in a hallway with her at some point. You end with the sentence she used on every desk sergeant who ever sighed down the phone at her: they will listen to you, they just have to be taught how.

choices.text: Continue Glenda's calls and complaints
choices.consequence: You inherit her envelope of numbers and keep making the calls. Some of them, now, get returned the same afternoon.

choices.text: Step back; let younger neighbors take it on
choices.consequence: You hand the envelope to a woman from the tenants' association who is thirty-four and angrier than you have been in a decade.

nodes.text: Bottom drawer of the dresser, under the winter things. The composition book has gone soft at the corners and the ink on the first page has browned. Two entries from the March before anybody believed a word of it. You sit on the end of the bed with it open across your knees and decide whether this is a thing you keep or a thing you hand on. Either way, you were there, and you said so.

choices.text: Keep the notebook in the drawer
choices.consequence: You put it back under the sweaters. Some evidence has done its work and is allowed, afterwards, to just be yours.

choices.text: Give it to a neighbor who is starting hers
choices.consequence: You give it to a young woman on the second floor who has started writing dates on her calendar, and you tell her to keep two copies.

nodes.text: Your name ends up in three policy footnotes and one foundation's annual report. You read them exactly once each. Your son grows up and becomes, against every plan he announced at nineteen, a social worker doing home visits in the same half of the city. The notebook lives in a box at the back of the closet. Some nights the sound of a stairwell door still wakes you, and you go back to sleep, and the sleep holds.

You keep the numbers in a binder with tabs and dates. When a neighbour knocks and starts a sentence with I know this sounds crazy, you put the kettle on and find a pen. When a new commander arrives at the precinct you go in, shake his hand, and learn his face so that he knows he has been learned. Vigilance turns out not to be courage at all. It is only the refusal to forget on schedule.
